title: EXAONE Demand 1.0: A Time Series Foundation Model for Demand Forecasting
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 25 Sep 2026]
    Title:EXAONE Demand 1.0: A Time Series Foundation Model for Demand Forecasting
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are pretrained on series from diverse domains, where demand series make up only a small fraction. Demand data has properties that such corpora rarely contain: Short histories, frequent zeros, censoring by stock-outs, and exogenous events that the series does not record. To this end, we propose EXAONE Demand, built on 1) a demand-specific corpus and 2) a demand-aware adapter. For the corpus, we assemble 11.3M series and 48.4B observations from 73 sources, and a synthetic generator supplies the behaviour that open demand data under-represents. For the adapter, we attach low-rank branches to a frozen general-domain backbone, one for each of the four demand classes (smooth, intermittent, erratic, and lumpy), and a router that reads eight scale-free statistics of the input series decides how much each branch contributes. We build EXAONE Demand in two versions, one trained on real-world and synthetic demand together and one trained on the synthetic corpus alone. On 22 held-out datasets, both versions outperform 36 TSFMs, and real-world demand adds a gain over synthetic data alone.

report.summary: EXAONE Demand 1.0 pairs a demand-specific pretraining corpus with a demand-aware adapter, beating 36 time series foundation models across 22 held-out datasets.
report.background: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as Chronos, TimesFM, Moirai and Lag-Llama are pretrained on large, heterogeneous corpora dominated by energy, traffic, weather and finance series. Demand data — retail sales, SKU-level orders, spare parts — is a tiny slice of those corpora and behaves differently: histories are short, zeros are frequent, demand is censored whenever a stock-out hides true demand, and promotions, holidays or competitor moves never appear as columns. Classical tools like Croston's method, SBA and TSB handle intermittency heuristically but cannot exploit large-scale pretraining. EXAONE Demand, from the EXAONE model family, argues the gap is not just a modeling problem but a data-representation problem, and attacks both sides at once.
key_points: A demand-specific corpus: the authors assembled 11.3M series and 48.4B observations drawn from 73 sources, then added a synthetic generator to cover behaviours that openly available demand data under-represents, such as extreme zero runs and censored peaks.

A demand-aware adapter instead of full retraining: low-rank branches are attached to a frozen general-domain backbone, with one branch per demand class — smooth, intermittent, erratic and lumpy — so specialised capacity is added cheaply.

A router decides the mixture: eight scale-free statistics of the input series are read at inference time to weight how much each branch contributes, letting one model serve very different demand patterns without class labels.

Two training recipes were tested — real plus synthetic demand, and synthetic only. Both beat 36 competing TSFMs on 22 held-out datasets, and adding real-world demand produced a further gain over synthetic data alone.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is another signal that general-purpose foundation models are being unbundled into vertical, domain-aware systems, and that the moat is increasingly the curated corpus plus lightweight adaptation rather than raw parameter count. For developers, the frozen-backbone plus low-rank-branch pattern is attractive: it keeps training and serving costs low, supports per-class specialisation, and offers a template for other messy domains such as insurance claims or clinical event streams. For regular users, the payoff is practical — better SKU-level forecasts mean less dead stock, fewer stock-outs and less spoilage. The caveat is that synthetic data cannot fully replace real demand, so the approach still depends on access to proprietary sales histories.
report.tools: To follow up, look at open TSFMs for comparison and baselines: Amazon's Chronos, Google's TimesFM, Salesforce's Moirai, and Lag-Llama. For pipelines and evaluation, GluonTS, Nixtla's NeuralForecast and StatsForecast (Croston, SBA, TSB baselines), and sktime are the standard toolkits; intermittent-demand metrics such as MASE, sCRPS and pinball loss are worth tracking on your own SKU data.
